report:
### Conclusion
The claim is **supported by strong scientific evidence**. In pregnant women with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) and high viral load, initiating tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) in the third trimester significantly reduces mother-to-child transmission (MTCT).

### Key Evidence
1. **High Efficacy**: Pregnant women with high HBV DNA levels ($\ge 200,000\text{ IU/mL}$) remain at elevated risk for vertical transmission even when infants receive standard birth immunoprophylaxis (HBV vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin). Clinical trials demonstrate that TDF initiated around weeks 28–32 of gestation rapidly suppresses maternal viral load prior to delivery, reducing infant infection rates to near zero.
2. **Global Guidelines**: Based on systematic reviews, the World Health Organization (WHO) and major hepatology guidelines recommend TDF prophylaxis in the third trimester for pregnant women meeting viral load or HBeAg-positivity thresholds.
3. **Safety Profile & Considerations**: Evidence shows TDF is well tolerated, with no significant increase in adverse maternal or fetal outcomes or congenital malformations. Clinical monitoring is recommended postpartum because stopping antiviral therapy can occasionally trigger maternal hepatitis flares. In addition, TDF complements—but does not replace—timely infant administration of the birth-dose vaccine.

### Sources
* WHO Guidelines on Antiviral Prophylaxis in Pregnancy: https://www.aidsdatahub.org/sites/default/files/resource/who-pmtct-hepatitis-b-virus-2020.pdf
* WHO Q&A on Preventing Mother-to-Child HBV Transmission: https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/hepatitis-preventing-mother-to-child-transmission-of-the-hepatitis-b-virus
* Review on Benefits and Risks of Antiviral Treatment in Pregnancy: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8198811/
* Clinical Evidence on Antiviral Therapy for Perinatal Transmission: https://www.e-cmh.org/journal/view.php?doi=10.3350/cmh.2017.0082
